extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of literary criticism; poetry readers and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for reading, judging, and criticizing poetry, focusing on belief, sincerity, technical presuppositions, and common critical preconceptions. Emphasizes close reading and testing critical theories against the poem as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief: emotional vs intellectual
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between intellectual belief (justified by logical place in an ordered system of ideas) and emotional belief (acceptance of an idea because it meets our needs and is implicated in our activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional belief is justified by success in meeting needs and may be given to ideas that are intellectually unbelievable; good poetry often evokes emotional belief without raising the question of intellectual belief. Readers may withhold intellectual assent yet give full emotional belief, and the critic should recognise the two kinds of belief and avoid conflating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding the arising of intellectual disbelief when reading
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading well 'the question of belief or disbelief, in the intellectual sense, never arises.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If intellectual disbelief is provoked (by the poet's fault or the reader's), the reader ceases to be reading poetry and shifts into another intellectual activity (e.g., astronomy, theology). Aim for readings that keep intellectual-system conflicts from interrupting poetic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity (multiple senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'sincere' has several senses: (a) ordinary business sincerity (not attempting to deceive); (b) self-deceptive insincerity (mistaking one's own motives); (c) discrepancy between a poem's claim on readers and the poet's shaping impulses; (d) an ideal sense of absolute freedom from impurity or interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism must specify which sense of sincerity is intended. A poem may be written for money or ambition and still be 'sincere' if external motives do not interfere with its growth; irony or contrary professed feeling is not necessarily insincere. The shaping impulses are the relevant standard for judging insincerity in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional genuineness / authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincere emotions may be judged as 'genuine' or 'spurious' in several possible senses: ideal-perfect-mind genuineness; simplicity/spontaneity opposed to sophistication; or authenticity measured by standards beyond suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal sense is a useful standard but unattainable; the 'simplicity' sense is common but unreliable (some simple-seeming emotions are artful). Criticism should be cautious about praising simplicity-as-sincerity and should seek more dependable standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards 'beyond suspicion' for testing sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use certain simple, definite responses as benchmarks of sincerity — responses 'beyond suspicion' — to help judge less certain poetic responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards suggests using pains/aversion like 'hate a bad smell' or responses evoked by contemplations such as: (i) man's loneliness; (ii) facts of birth and death; (iii) immensity of the universe; (iv) man's place in time; (v) enormity of his ignorance. Such responses can serve as reliable comparators when uncertain about a poem's sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical presuppositions must be judged relative to aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not suppose that the means a poet uses (rhymes, metre, form, sound devices) are valuable for their own sake or can be prescribed without reference to the poet's aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is a blunder to assign marks to details independently of the whole final result. Critics should avoid evaluating technical features in isolation and should determine how a detail contributes to the poem's overall effect and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfection of rhyme (Imperfect Rhymes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often object to imperfect rhymes as a technical fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imperfection of rhyme should not be condemned automatically; its value depends on its relation to the poem's aims and overall effect. See protocols/examples referenced (2.1-2.22, 3.1, 3.41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical irregularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms often target metrical irregularities as faults in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate irregularities in the context of the poem: they may be justified by, or integral to, the poem's purposes. Examples cited include (2.2, 3.44, 8.44, 12.51, 13.61, 13.62).

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-end stop (caesura/lineation choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections are frequently made to the placement of line-end stops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge lineation choices with regard to the poem's rhythm, sense, and intention rather than by an independent rule. Examples: (8.33, 8.43).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonnet Form
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations about definite sonnet divisions and forms are technical presuppositions readers may bring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insist on rigid formal divisions as absolute; sonnet variations may be valid if they serve the poem's aim. Examples include (3.1, 3.4, 3.41, 5.56, 6.4, 9.82, 12.51).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cacophony
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of harsh, discordant sound patterns is often criticised as cacophony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cacophony is not automatically bad; its appropriateness depends on whether it suits the poem's purpose. Protocol examples: (2.23, 3.4, 6.33, 10.42, 10.44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euphony
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasant, harmonious sound (euphony) is often prized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euphony is desirable only insofar as it fits the poem's requirements; it can be misapplied as an independent test. Examples: (4.22, 7.57).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic qualities of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics sometimes ascribe fixed 'intrinsic' qualities to words (e.g., certain words being inherently beautiful or ugly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of treating word qualities as absolute; their effect depends on context and the poem's overall design. See references (10.4, 10.55).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Demands that a poem's descriptive elements be strictly accurate (factual or observational correctness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive accuracy is relevant only insofar as the poem requires it; many poetic purposes tolerate or require departures from literal accuracy. Examples: (2.22, 8.15, 9.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of vivid, striking description is often demanded as a virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vividness may be important but is not universally required; it must be judged against the poem's aims. Example cited: (11.22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic (coherence of reasoning within poem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers may insist on logical consistency in the poem's development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic matters when the poem's nature demands it; some poetry intentionally departs from ordinary logical sequence for effect. Example: (2.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unmixed metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism often objects to mixing metaphors or incoherent figurative language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blanket condemnation; presence of mixed metaphor must be assessed for its effect and whether it undermines the poem's aims. References: (6.41, 10.61).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems of figurative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Various issues arising from metaphor, simile, and other figures of speech are grounds for critical attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze figurative language in terms of its contribution to overall meaning and effect; see Part III, Chapter 2 for detailed discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand that a poem be clear in sense or expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity is sometimes required but not always; some poems aim at obscurity or ambiguity deliberately. Assess whether clarity is essential given the poem's aims. References: (5.51, 6.37).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtue of economy in expression and avoidance of unnecessary verbosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness may be desirable in many contexts but is not an absolute; judge by the poem's needs. Example: (13.65).

rubrics_metrics.name: Majesty in epitaphs
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific stylistic demand that epitaphs (and similar forms) achieve a certain 'majestic' tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specialty demand is relevant to genre; assess whether majesty suits the particular epitaph rather than imposing it universally. Example: (11.43).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for a 'serious' subject or message
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers expect poetry to have a serious subject or to 'say' something important; this is a common preconception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'saying' as 'communicate' (many poems do) from 'state' (many great poems state nothing). Do not reduce value to whether an isolated important statement is present; assess the poem's result as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lilt (musical 'lilt' as independent test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for a musical lilt or swing in a poem is often treated as a test for value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lilt is valuable only when required by and conditioned to the rest of the poem; as an independent demand it blinds readers to other important movements. See (4.16, 4.22, 8.43, 12.41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying crude 'subject' or 'message' theories directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories that reduce poetic value to the presence of a subject or inspirational message lead to indiscriminate judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such crude preconceptions enable quick but often mistaken conclusions; more refined, discriminating preconceptions cannot be directly applied either. Critics should seek understanding of complexities and conditionalities rather than simple keys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware shorthand confusions between poem's effects and poem's structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics often use shorthand (e.g., attributing rhythm, meanings, or beauty to the poem itself) which identifies effects on readers with characteristics of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shorthand can make critics revert to obsolete attitudes about language. When judging, unpack the shorthand: distinguish the poem's effects on readers from structural properties and test claims against evidence rather than assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess influence of prior expectations rather than stated reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: A good reader can give inept stated reasons for a correct judgment; what matters is the actual influence of prior expectations on reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should examine how illegitimate expectations (technical presuppositions or preconceptions) have shaped a reader's response, rather than taking stated reasons at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial motive vs shaping impulse
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish external motives (money, pique, ambition) from the poet's shaping impulses; only the shaping impulses are relevant to judging sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem may be composed for extrinsic reasons yet be artistically valid if those motives do not interfere with its growth. Conversely, desires to be 'original' or 'poetic' often cause insincerity by interfering with shaping impulses.
